description.value: The study examined common and distinct neural responses to personally relevant affect labeling and cognitive reappraisal of aversive images in healthy older adults.

value: We hypothesized that personally-relevant affect labeling and reappraisal would engage multiple overlapping lateral prefrontal regulatory regions, including VLPFC, and result in decreased amygdala responses and self-reported distress.
We also hypothesized that reappraisal would result in more widespread prefrontal activation than affect labeling because it seems to represent a more complex effortful psychological process

description.value: A cross-sectional study of healthy older adults who completed one fMRI session before a subsequent 8-week mindfulness-based stress reduction intervention.

name.value: fMRI affect labeling and reappraisal task

spans.text: #### fMRI affect labeling and reappraisal task

description.value: Participants viewed negative emotionally evocative scenes and either observed them, labeled their own emotional response, reappraised them, or performed a shape-matching control task.
Participants passively viewed a single negative emotionally evocative scene for 6 seconds and were told simply to look at the picture; no response or regulation demand was required.

Participants viewed a single negative emotionally evocative scene for 6 seconds and selected, by button press, the word that best matched their own emotional response from three options drawn from Sad, Anxious, Disgusted, and Other. Other was always available for emotions not represented or for no emotional response.

Participants viewed a single negative emotionally evocative scene for 6 seconds and intentionally used cognitive reappraisal to decrease their emotional response by thinking about the image in less distressing terms, such as imagining a positive outcome or viewing it as a fictional movie scene.

Participants viewed a target geometric shape and selected by button press, from three options at the bottom of the screen, the shape matching the target; this was a non-emotional cognitive-motor control condition.

spans.text: While being scanned, participants were shown photographs of negative emotionally-evocative scenes (from the International Affective Picture System; IAPS; Lang et al.,  2008 , as described below) presented in a blocked design and were instructed to either passively view the stimuli, or use one of two emotion regulation strategies, affect labeling or reappraisal.
Stimuli were presented on a Macintosh computer using MacStim 3.2.1 software

stimuli.value: Negative emotionally evocative scenes from the International Affective Picture System.

spans.text: Button press responses were collected using an MR-compatible button box connected to the Macintosh.

instructions.value: Participants viewed negative emotionally evocative scenes in blocked trials and were instructed either to passively observe each image, label their own emotional response by selecting the best-matching word from three options, or use cognitive reappraisal to decrease their emotional response by thinking about each image in less distressing terms. Participants practiced all conditions before scanning. After each block, they rated average unpleasantness from 0 (not at all unpleasant) to 3 (severely unpleasant).
